patient.name: Tomasz Nowak
patient.setting: Emergency Department, then the hepatology ward
patient.complaint: Swollen abdomen and breathlessness lying flat for 6 weeks
background: Alcohol-related cirrhosis diagnosed 2 years ago; still drinks 3 cans of lager a day
Builder from Ealing; trousers no longer fasten

diagnosis.exam: Expect 'Which is the most likely diagnosis?' or 'most likely finding' with a drinker with abdominal distension and shifting dullness; and the emergency twist of ascites + fever + abdominal pain = spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.

points: Six weeks of a **painless, swelling abdomen**.
Breathless when lying flat; sleeps propped up.

steps.lead: Tomasz's cirrhosis has raised his portal pressure: fluid is collecting in his **peritoneal cavity**.
**Cirrhosis** is by far the commonest cause; Tomasz's drinking is the driver. Malignancy is the main other cause to consider.

visual.title: Where the fluid sits
visual.caption: Lying flat, fluid sinks to the flanks: dull flanks, resonant centre (gas-filled bowel floats up).

points: Dull flanks that become resonant when he rolls over: **shifting dullness**.
Fluid thrill present; dilated superficial veins.
Spider naevi, palmar erythema, splenomegaly hard to feel.

steps.lead: Tomasz shows the classic picture: painless distension, weight gain, breathlessness, **shifting dullness**, a fluid thrill, oedema and other chronic liver disease signs.

steps.q: Three days later Tomasz spikes 38.3°C with diffuse abdominal pain and becomes muddled. What must you suspect?
steps.r: Ascites + fever + abdominal pain (and new confusion) = **SBP** until proven otherwise.

steps.lead: Tomasz now has the triad of ascites, **fever and abdominal pain**: SBP, a medical emergency.
Infected ascites is the key complication. In Tomasz the only sign may be new confusion or worsening kidneys, so the threshold to tap is low.

steps.text: SBP can be **subtle**: no peritonism, just fever, confusion or a rise in creatinine. Tap every cirrhotic with ascites who is unwell.

investigation.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial/diagnostic investigation?': ultrasound to detect ascites, and a diagnostic tap within 8 hours for suspected SBP (neutrophils above 250 cells/mm³); then use the SAAG to find the cause.

steps.lead: Tomasz's **abdominal ultrasound** confirms ascites (and shows a small, nodular liver). It is both the first test and the gold standard for detecting fluid.

steps.q: Tomasz is febrile with abdominal pain. What is the most important next test?
steps.r: A **diagnostic paracentesis** within 8 hours: the neutrophil count makes or breaks SBP.

steps.lead: Tomasz has **LFTs, U&Es and INR** sent and a **diagnostic tap within 8 hours** of suspected SBP. A raised INR does not stop a diagnostic tap.

steps.title: Tomasz's ascitic tap and bloods
steps.text: Neutrophils above 250 confirm SBP; culture is often negative, so do not wait for it.

visual.title: Ascitic neutrophil count
visual.label: Tomasz 620
visual.caption: Above 250 cells/mm³ is SBP, whatever the culture shows.

steps.lead: Tomasz's neutrophils are **620**: SBP. His SAAG is 27 − 8 g/L = 1.9 g/dL, so his ascites is **portal hypertensive**.

visual.title: SAAG (serum minus ascitic albumin)
visual.label: Tomasz 1.9
visual.caption: High gradient = transudate from portal hypertension: cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari, right heart failure, constrictive pericarditis.

steps.text: Work the SAAG in g/dL: serum albumin 27 g/L (2.7) minus ascitic 8 g/L (0.8) = **1.9**. Anything **≥1.1** means portal hypertension.

management.exam: Expect 'Which is the most appropriate initial management?': salt restriction and spironolactone first-line, large-volume paracentesis with albumin for tense ascites, TIPS if refractory, and IV antibiotics plus albumin for SBP.

steps.lead: Tomasz has SBP: **IV ceftriaxone** now, plus **HAS 1.5 g/kg** in the first 6 hours and **1 g/kg on day 3** to protect his kidneys.

steps.title: SBP bundle
steps.caption: Do not wait for culture to start antibiotics.

points: Fever settles by day 3; creatinine back to 92.
Abdomen still **tense**; he cannot lie flat.

steps.q: Tomasz's tense ascites is splinting his diaphragm. What gives fastest relief?
steps.r: **Large-volume paracentesis** with IV human albumin cover relieves tense ascites within hours.

steps.lead: Tomasz has 8 litres drained with **HAS cover**, which prevents circulatory dysfunction. He has no DIC, so drainage is safe.
To stop it re-accumulating Tomasz must **stop alcohol**, cut salt and start **spironolactone 100 mg**, titrating to 400 mg, with furosemide.

visual.title: Tomasz's weight on diuretics
visual.caption: Steady loss of about 0.5 kg a day on spironolactone and salt restriction.

steps.text: Watch for **hyperkalaemia** and **hyponatraemia** on spironolactone, and gynaecomastia long-term. Check U&Es regularly.

steps.lead: If Tomasz's ascites keeps returning despite maximal diuretics, he is referred for **TIPS** (and assessed for transplant).
Tomasz's care follows **NICE NG50** and **BSG** ascites guidance, including antibiotic prophylaxis after his SBP.

science.exam: Expect applied questions: why fluid collects (hydrostatic and oncotic), why spironolactone is first-line (secondary hyperaldosteronism), what the SAAG means, and why albumin is given with paracentesis.

steps.lead: Tomasz's scarred liver raises **sinusoidal pressure** and makes little albumin: high hydrostatic, low oncotic pressure push fluid into the peritoneum.

steps.title: Why Tomasz retains salt and water

steps.lead: Tomasz's kidneys sense underfilling and switch on **RAAS**; spironolactone blocks the aldosterone that is holding on to his sodium.
Tomasz's high SAAG means his fluid is a **transudate** driven by portal pressure, not an exudate from cancer or infection.

steps.q: How did bacteria reach Tomasz's ascites?
o: Translocation across an oedematous gut wall
steps.r: **Bacterial translocation** across an oedematous, hypomotile gut into fluid with poor opsonic activity: hence gut organisms (E. coli).

steps.lead: Tomasz's oedematous, sluggish gut lets **gut bacteria translocate** into ascites that has little opsonic defence.
Drain 8 litres from Tomasz without albumin and his splanchnic bed dilates further: **paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunction**, renal failure and higher mortality.

mcq.q: What is the most common cause of ascites?
Which examination sign is classic for ascites?
Which triad suggests spontaneous bacterial peritonitis?
mcq.r: **Ascites + fever + abdominal pain** = SBP until proven otherwise.

mcq.q: Which is the initial and gold-standard test to detect ascites?
Which ascitic neutrophil count diagnoses SBP?
A SAAG of 1.8 g/dL suggests which cause?

mcq.r: **Spironolactone 100 mg**, titrated to 400 mg, with furosemide.

mcq.q: What must be given with large-volume paracentesis?
Which is the treatment for refractory ascites?
Why is spironolactone effective in cirrhotic ascites?
mcq.r: **RAAS** is activated by effective arterial underfilling; spironolactone antagonises aldosterone.

prompts.q: What is ascites, and what causes it?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: one cause dominates the papers.

points.p: Abnormal fluid in the peritoneal cavity
points.why: Ultrasound detects as little as 100 mL.

points.p: Most commonly portal hypertension from cirrhosis
points.why: Alcohol is the usual cause of the cirrhosis.

points.p: Malignancy is the other important cause
points.why: Low SAAG; think ovarian or GI primary.

prompts.q: What are the symptoms and examination signs of ascites?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: how you prove fluid at the bedside.

points.p: Abdominal distension, discomfort and weight gain
Breathlessness with large-volume ascites
Shifting dullness
Fluid thrill
Superficial veins, peripheral oedema, chronic liver disease signs
points.why: Signs of portal hypertension and liver disease.

prompts.q: What is the key emergency complication of ascites and how does it present?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: ascites plus something new and unwell.

points.p: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis (SBP)
Ascites, fever and abdominal pain
Abdominal distension and tenderness; can be subtle (confusion, AKI)
points.why: Tap any unwell cirrhotic with ascites.

prompts.q: How do you tell ascites from other causes of a distended abdomen?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: the five Fs, by percussion.

points.p: Ascites: dull flanks, resonant centre, shifting dullness
Obstruction (flatus): hyperresonant, colicky pain, vomiting
Mass (e.g. ovarian): dull centre, resonant flanks

prompts.q: Which investigations confirm ascites and diagnose SBP?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: image to detect it, tap to diagnose infection.

points.p: Ultrasound abdomen: initial and gold standard for detecting ascites
Bloods: LFTs, U&Es, INR
Diagnostic paracentesis within 8 hours of suspected SBP
SBP if ascitic neutrophils above 250 cells/mm³

prompts.q: What is the SAAG, what are the cut-offs, and what does each mean?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: subtract, then compare to 1.1.

points.p: SAAG = serum albumin minus ascitic albumin
≥1.1 g/dL = portal hypertension (cirrhosis, Budd-Chiari, right HF, constrictive pericarditis)
<1.1 g/dL = non-portal (peritoneal carcinomatosis, TB)

prompts.q: What is the first-line management of cirrhotic ascites, with doses?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: cause, salt, then one named diuretic.

points.p: Treat the cause: stop alcohol, manage cirrhosis
Dietary salt restriction with high-energy, high-protein diet
Spironolactone 100 mg OD titrated to 400 mg
With furosemide
points.why: Added for effect and to balance potassium.

prompts.q: How do you manage tense, refractory ascites and SBP?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: drain with albumin; shunt if it keeps coming back; antibiotics plus albumin for SBP.

points.p: Large-volume paracentesis with IV human albumin solution
Paracentesis contraindicated in DIC
points.why: Bleeding gums, high D-dimer, low fibrinogen.

points.p: Refractory ascites: TIPS
SBP: IV antibiotics such as ceftriaxone
SBP: HAS 1.5 g/kg in 6 hours, then 1 g/kg on day 3

prompts.q: Why does portal hypertension cause ascites, and why use spironolactone?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: Starling forces, then the kidney.

points.p: Raised hydrostatic pressure in the splanchnic/sinusoidal circulation
Low albumin reduces oncotic pressure
Splanchnic vasodilation causes effective arterial underfilling, activating RAAS
Spironolactone antagonises aldosterone

prompts.q: How does SBP develop, and why give albumin with large-volume paracentesis?
prompts.tip: Exam thinking: gut bacteria in; circulating volume out.

points.p: Bacterial translocation across an oedematous, hypomotile gut wall
points.why: Hence gut organisms: E. coli, Klebsiella.

points.p: Ascitic fluid has reduced opsonic/antibacterial activity
Without albumin, fluid removal worsens splanchnic vasodilation and effective circulating volume
High SAAG = transudate from portal pressure; low = exudate
points.why: The SAAG tells you the mechanism.

glossary.Ascites: Abnormal collection of fluid in the peritoneal cavity, most often from portal hypertension in cirrhosis.
glossary.Peritoneal cavity: The space between the two layers of peritoneum lining the abdomen and covering the gut.
glossary.Portal hypertension: Raised pressure in the portal vein, usually from a scarred cirrhotic liver resisting blood flow.
glossary.Cirrhosis: End-stage liver scarring with nodules, causing portal hypertension and liver failure.
glossary.Shifting dullness: Flank dullness that moves to the uppermost side becoming resonant when the patient rolls: proves free fluid.
glossary.Fluid thrill: A tap on one flank felt as a wave on the other, seen in large-volume ascites.
glossary.Everted umbilicus: Belly button pushed outwards by raised intra-abdominal pressure.
glossary.Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: Infection of ascitic fluid without a surgical source, diagnosed by ascitic neutrophils above 250 cells/mm³.
glossary.SBP: Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis: infected ascites, a medical emergency.
glossary.Secondary peritonitis: Peritonitis from a surgical source such as perforation; usually polymicrobial with free air.
glossary.Paracentesis: Putting a needle or drain into the peritoneal cavity to sample or remove ascitic fluid.
glossary.Diagnostic tap: A small-volume paracentesis to send fluid for cell count, albumin and culture.
glossary.Large-volume paracentesis: Draining several litres of ascites to relieve tense distension, given with albumin cover.
glossary.SAAG: Serum-ascites albumin gradient: serum minus ascitic albumin; 1.1 g/dL or more means portal hypertension.
glossary.Transudate: Low-protein fluid pushed out by pressure, as in portal hypertension.
glossary.Exudate: High-protein fluid from inflammation or malignancy that leaks through damaged vessels.
glossary.Peritoneal carcinomatosis: Cancer spread across the peritoneum, causing low-SAAG malignant ascites.
glossary.Budd-Chiari syndrome: Hepatic vein obstruction causing hepatomegaly, abdominal pain and high-SAAG ascites.
glossary.Constrictive pericarditis: Stiff, scarred pericardium restricting heart filling, raising venous pressure and causing ascites.
glossary.HAS: Human albumin solution, given IV to support circulating volume in paracentesis and SBP.
glossary.Human albumin solution: Intravenous albumin used to protect circulation and kidneys in liver patients.
glossary.Spironolactone: Aldosterone antagonist diuretic, first-line for cirrhotic ascites.
glossary.Furosemide: Loop diuretic added to spironolactone for ascites.
glossary.TIPS: Transjugular intrahepatic portosystemic shunt: a stent linking portal and hepatic veins to lower portal pressure.
glossary.DIC: Disseminated intravascular coagulation: widespread clotting and bleeding, with high D-dimer and low fibrinogen.
glossary.Ceftriaxone: Third-generation cephalosporin antibiotic used IV to treat SBP.
glossary.RAAS: Renin-angiotensin-aldosterone system, which makes the kidneys retain sodium and water.
glossary.Secondary hyperaldosteronism: High aldosterone driven by low effective circulating volume, as in cirrhosis.
glossary.Splanchnic vasodilation: Widening of gut blood vessels in cirrhosis, which leaves the rest of the circulation underfilled.
glossary.Effective arterial underfilling: Arteries feel underfilled despite total body fluid overload, triggering salt and water retention.
glossary.Oncotic pressure: Pulling pressure of plasma proteins, mainly albumin, that keeps fluid inside vessels.
glossary.Hydrostatic pressure: Pushing pressure of fluid within vessels that drives it out into tissues.
glossary.Bacterial translocation: Gut bacteria crossing the bowel wall into lymph nodes, blood or ascites.
glossary.Opsonic activity: The ability of fluid proteins such as complement to coat bacteria for killing by phagocytes.
glossary.Paracentesis-induced circulatory dysfunc: Circulatory collapse and renal impairment after large-volume drainage without albumin cover.
glossary.Hepatorenal syndrome: Kidney failure caused by severe liver disease and splanchnic vasodilation.
glossary.Spider naevi: Small red spots with radiating vessels on the upper body, a sign of chronic liver disease.
glossary.Palmar erythema: Red palms, a sign of chronic liver disease.
glossary.NICE NG50: NICE guideline on assessing and managing cirrhosis in people over 16.

technique.stem: A 56 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis and ascites has 2 days of diffuse abdominal pain and feeling unwell. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 104 bpm and BP 102/64 mmHg. His abdomen is distended and diffusely tender with shifting dullness. Erect chest X-ray shows no free air.
technique.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?

steps.x: Diagnosis: an unwell patient with known ascites.
Ascites + fever + abdominal pain; no perforation.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Cholecystitis gives localised RUQ pain and Murphy's sign.
Hepatorenal syndrome is renal failure, not fever and pain.
TB peritonitis is subacute with weight loss and low SAAG.
No haematemesis or melaena.

steps.x: **C. Spontaneous bacterial peritonitis.** Rule: ascites + fever + pain = SBP.

technique.stem: A 63 year old woman with cirrhosis and ascites has become confused with a temperature of 37.9°C. A diagnostic paracentesis is performed within 2 hours of arrival.
technique.q: Which ascitic fluid result best confirms the suspected diagnosis?

steps.x: Subtle SBP: confusion and low-grade fever.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Amylase is for pancreatic ascites.
Low glucose suggests secondary peritonitis but does not define SBP.
Protein helps assess risk, not diagnose SBP.
Triglycerides identify chylous ascites.

technique.stem: A 59 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has needed large-volume paracentesis every 2 weeks for 3 months. He takes spironolactone 400 mg daily and furosemide, follows a low-salt diet and has stopped drinking. His BP is 110/70 mmHg and pulse rate 80 bpm.
technique.q: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

steps.x: Next step when ascites keeps returning.
Maximal diuretics, salt restriction and abstinence have failed: **refractory ascites**.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Albumin cover must not be dropped; it prevents circulatory dysfunction.
Biopsy does not treat ascites.
Ciprofloxacin is SBP prophylaxis, not ascites control.
Propranolol is for varices and may worsen refractory ascites.

technique.stem: A 54 year old woman with cirrhosis has 9 litres of tense ascites drained. The registrar gives intravenous human albumin solution during the procedure. A student asks why.
technique.q: Which is the main reason albumin is given?

steps.x: Mechanism: why albumin with large-volume drainage?
Rapid loss of a large volume in someone already vasodilated.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking
steps.x: Albumin keeps fluid in vessels, preventing **circulatory dysfunction** and renal failure.

elim: Albumin has no effect on glucose.
Antibiotics, not albumin, prevent SBP.
Albumin contains no clotting factors; FFP does.
Lactulose treats encephalopathy.

practice.stem: A 60 year old man who drinks a bottle of whisky a day has 6 weeks of increasing abdominal swelling. He has palmar erythema and spider naevi. His pulse rate is 86 bpm and BP 112/70 mmHg. His abdomen is distended and nontender.
practice.q: Which is the most likely finding on abdominal percussion?
practice.e: Ascites from alcoholic cirrhosis gives dull flanks that shift when the patient rolls: shifting dullness. Central dullness with resonant flanks suggests a mass such as an ovarian cyst.

steps.x: Chronic liver disease + painless distension = ascites.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: That is the pattern of a large central mass.
Hyperresonance is gas: obstruction.
A pulsatile mass is an aneurysm.
Visible peristalsis is obstruction.

practice.stem: A 57 year old woman with cirrhosis and ascites has 1 day of abdominal pain and fever. Her temperature is 38.5°C, pulse rate 110 bpm, BP 98/60 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her abdomen is distended and diffusely tender. Erect chest X-ray shows no free air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
practice.e: Ascites, fever and pain with ascitic neutrophils above 250 and a single Gram-negative organism, with no free air, is SBP. Secondary peritonitis implies a perforation, usually polymicrobial with free air.

steps.x: Classic triad; tap neutrophils 540; single Gram-negative organism.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Appendicitis gives RIF pain, not diffuse tenderness with infected ascites.
Amylase is normal.
Carcinomatosis is not acute with fever.
No free air or polymicrobial picture to suggest perforation.

steps.x: **E. SBP.** Rule: >250 neutrophils, no surgical source.

practice.stem: A 55 year old man has 2 months of abdominal distension. He drank heavily for 20 years. There is shifting dullness and splenomegaly. Ultrasound shows a small nodular liver and ascites. A diagnostic tap is performed.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his ascites?
practice.e: SAAG is 2.9 − 0.9 = 2.0 g/dL (≥1.1), so portal hypertension; with a small nodular liver and splenomegaly in a drinker, it is cirrhosis. Carcinomatosis and TB give a SAAG below 1.1.

steps.x: Cause of ascites: calculate the SAAG.
Cirrhosis with portal hypertension; labs: SAAG 2.0, normal neutrophils, negative cytology.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Nephrotic syndrome gives a low SAAG with heavy proteinuria and normal liver.
Pancreatic ascites has high amylase and low SAAG.
Carcinomatosis gives low SAAG and positive cytology.
TB gives low SAAG and lymphocytes.

steps.x: **A. Cirrhosis with portal hypertension.** Rule: SAAG ≥1.1 = portal.

practice.stem: A 62 year old man with cirrhosis and ascites has fever and abdominal tenderness. A diagnostic tap shows 780 neutrophils/mm³ and a Gram stain shows Gram-negative rods. There is no free air on erect chest X-ray.
practice.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
practice.e: SBP is usually caused by gut Gram-negative organisms that translocate across the bowel wall, most commonly E. coli (then Klebsiella).

steps.x: SBP with Gram-negative rods: gut bacteria.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Candida is a yeast, not a Gram-negative rod.
TB gives lymphocytic, low-SAAG ascites.
Staph aureus is a Gram-positive coccus.
Strep pyogenes is a Gram-positive coccus.

practice.stem: A 68 year old woman has 3 months of abdominal distension, early satiety and 8 kg weight loss. She drinks no alcohol. There is shifting dullness and no stigmata of chronic liver disease. Her pulse rate is 92 bpm and BP 124/76 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of her ascites?
practice.e: SAAG is 3.3 − 2.6 = 0.7 g/dL (<1.1), a non-portal cause; with weight loss and early satiety in an older woman, peritoneal carcinomatosis is most likely. The other options all give a high SAAG.

clues: early satiety and 8 kg weight loss
no stigmata of chronic liver disease
steps.x: Weight loss, no liver disease; labs: SAAG 0.7.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Budd-Chiari gives high SAAG with hepatomegaly and pain.
Cirrhosis gives high SAAG and liver stigmata.
Constrictive pericarditis gives high SAAG and raised JVP.
Right heart failure gives high SAAG and raised JVP.

steps.x: **D. Peritoneal carcinomatosis.** Rule: SAAG <1.1 = cancer or TB.

practice.stem: A 64 year old man with cirrhosis has become increasingly breathless over 3 weeks, worse lying flat. His abdomen is tense and grossly distended with shifting dullness. His chest is clear on auscultation. His temperature is 36.8°C, pulse rate 90 bpm, BP 108/68 mmHg and oxygen saturation 95% breathing air.
practice.q: Which is the most likely cause of his breathlessness?
practice.e: Tense, large-volume ascites pushes up and splints the diaphragm, causing breathlessness worse lying flat; it is relieved by paracentesis. The clear chest and absent fever argue against pneumonia and LVF.

steps.x: Cause of breathlessness in a cirrhotic.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Hepatopulmonary syndrome causes hypoxia worse sitting up (platypnoea), not orthopnoea with tense ascites.
LVF gives crackles; the chest is clear.
No fever and a clear chest.
PE is sudden with pleuritic pain or tachycardia.

practice.stem: A 58 year old man with heavy alcohol use has a distended abdomen. The doctor is unsure whether the distension is fluid or obesity. His pulse rate is 82 bpm and BP 126/80 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
practice.e: Ultrasound abdomen is both the initial investigation and the gold standard for detecting ascites, and can guide a tap. Abdominal X-ray is poor at showing fluid.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: AXR does not reliably show ascites.
CT shows it but is not first-line.
Laparoscopy is invasive.
MRI is not the first test.

practice.stem: A 61 year old woman with cirrhosis and ascites is admitted with new confusion and abdominal discomfort. Her temperature is 38.0°C, pulse rate 102 bpm and BP 104/62 mmHg. Her INR is 1.8.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
practice.e: Suspected SBP needs a diagnostic ascitic tap within 8 hours; neutrophils above 250 confirm it. A raised INR is not a reason to delay.

steps.x: Fever, confusion, ascites = SBP until proven otherwise.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: AXR does not diagnose SBP.
Blood cultures help but do not diagnose SBP alone.
Confusion here is from infection/encephalopathy; CT head is not first.
Erect CXR looks for perforation but the tap is diagnostic.

steps.x: **D. Diagnostic paracentesis.** INR is not a contraindication.

practice.stem: A 54 year old man with alcohol-related cirrhosis has moderate ascites. He has stopped drinking. His pulse rate is 78 bpm and BP 118/74 mmHg. His sodium, potassium and creatinine are normal.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate first-line drug treatment?
practice.e: With salt restriction, spironolactone 100 mg daily (titrated to 400 mg) is the first-line diuretic for cirrhotic ascites, with furosemide added. Furosemide alone is less effective.

steps.x: Normal electrolytes and renal function: safe to start.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Thiazides are not used for ascites.
Furosemide is an add-on, not first-line alone.
Indapamide is an antihypertensive.
Mannitol is for raised intracranial pressure.

practice.stem: A 66 year old woman with cirrhosis has tense ascites causing breathlessness and abdominal pain. She is on spironolactone and furosemide. Her pulse rate is 88 bpm and BP 110/68 mmHg. There is no fever and ascitic neutrophils are 60 cells/mm³. Clotting is stable with no bleeding.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Large-volume paracentesis with human albumin solution
practice.e: Tense, symptomatic ascites needs large-volume paracentesis with IV human albumin cover to prevent circulatory dysfunction. Diuretic changes are too slow; TIPS is for refractory ascites.

steps.x: Symptomatic tense ascites, no SBP, no DIC.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Too slow for tense, symptomatic ascites.
Without albumin risks circulatory dysfunction.
Transplant is not the immediate step.
TIPS is for refractory, recurrent ascites.

practice.stem: A 59 year old man with cirrhosis and ascites has fever and abdominal pain. A diagnostic tap shows 410 neutrophils/mm³. He weighs 70 kg. His temperature is 38.3°C, pulse rate 106 bpm and BP 100/62 mmHg.
practice.q: Which is the most appropriate initial management?
o: Intravenous ceftriaxone and human albumin solution
practice.e: SBP is treated with IV antibiotics (e.g. ceftriaxone) plus HAS 1.5 g/kg in the first 6 hours and 1 g/kg on day 3. Oral ciprofloxacin is prophylaxis after recovery.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Large-volume drainage is not the treatment for infection.
Oral ciprofloxacin is prophylaxis, not treatment.

practice.stem: A 57 year old man with cirrhosis and ascites has a low urinary sodium and high plasma renin and aldosterone despite total body fluid overload. He is started on spironolactone.
practice.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of benefit?
o: Antagonises aldosterone, opposing RAAS-driven sodium retention
Blocks carbonic anhydrase in the proximal tubule
Blocks NKCC2 in the loop of Henle
practice.e: Splanchnic vasodilation causes effective arterial underfilling, activating RAAS (secondary hyperaldosteronism). Spironolactone antagonises aldosterone in the collecting duct. NKCC2 is furosemide's target.

steps.t: Make your own answer before looking

elim: Carbonic anhydrase is acetazolamide.
NKCC2 is furosemide.
Diuretics do not change albumin synthesis.
Non-selective beta-blockers lower portal pressure, not spironolactone.
